pos: n. (the raised strip of earth between furrows)
etymology: Old English hrycg, the back of an animal, a ridge. In Psalm 65:10 it renders the Hebrew telem, a furrow, the ridge thrown up by the plough.
biblical_def: Psalm 65 is a harvest hymn, and David watches God farming the land Himself. “Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it” (Psalm 65:9). Then he comes down to the ploughed field: “Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:10). The farmer throws up the ridges and cuts the furrows; God sends the rain that soaks them, settles them and makes the seed spring. Webster cites this very verse for ridge as the strip between furrows. And the year's end is God's crown on it all: “Thou crownest the year with thy goodness; and thy paths drop fatness” (Psalm 65:11). Every ridge in every field is watered by the river of God, and every harvest is His gift before it is the farmer's wage.

webster_full: RIDGE, noun [Latin rugo.] 1. The back or top of the back.
2. A long or continued range of hills or mountains; or the upper part of such a range. We say, a long ridge of hills, or the highest ridge
3. A steep elevation, eminence or protuberance. Part rise in crystal wall, or ridge direct.
4. A long rising land, or a strip of ground thrown up by a plow or left between furrows. Psalms 65:10.
5. The top of the roof of a building.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. Modern readers attribute rain and harvest entirely to natural process, and Scripture does not deny secondary causes; it insists that God works through them, so that the farmer's ridge and the cloud's shower are both under His hand.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is thanksgiving for daily bread. God visits the earth; the ridges are watered abundantly; the year is crowned with His goodness.

pos: n. (a pile of sheaves or grain)
etymology: Old Norse stakkr, a haystack. In Exodus 22:6 it renders the Hebrew gadish, a heap of sheaves, a shock.
biblical_def: The law of Moses dealt with fire in the harvest field. “If fire break out, and catch in thorns, so that the stacks of corn, or the standing corn, or the field, be consumed therewith; he that kindled the fire shall surely make restitution” (Exodus 22:6). A man burning thorns on his own land answered for his neighbour's stacks if the fire spread. The verse before applies the same rule to straying cattle: “of the best of his own field, and of the best of his own vineyard, shall he make restitution” (Exodus 22:5). Negligence is not innocence; the man who starts the fire pays for the harvest it eats. Samson later turned the principle into a weapon, setting foxes with firebrands loose in the Philistines' grain: “he let them go into the standing corn of the Philistines, and burnt up both the shocks, and also the standing corn, with the vineyards and olives” (Judges 15:5). The law protected the stack; vengeance burned it.

In America, the stack differs from the cock only in size, both being conical.

In England, this distinction is not always observed.
This word in Great Britain is sometimes applied to a pile of wood containing 108 cubic feet, and also to a pile of poles; but I believe never in America.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The case laws of Exodus are often treated as primitive, but their principle of personal responsibility for negligent harm underlies the common law of torts in every Christian nation.

etymology: Old English socian, to soak, related to sucan, to suck. In Isaiah 34:7 it renders the Hebrew ravah, to be saturated, drink one's fill.
biblical_def: Isaiah 34 is the prophecy against Edom, and its imagery is a great sacrifice. “The sword of the LORD is filled with blood, it is made fat with fatness, and with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams: for the LORD hath a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Idumea” (Isaiah 34:6). The strong beasts fall with the weak: “And the unicorns shall come down with them, and the bullocks with the bulls; and their land shall be soaked with blood, and their dust made fat with fatness” (Isaiah 34:7). Webster quotes this verse under soak, to drench. The reason is given in the next line: “For it is the day of the LORD'S vengeance, and the year of recompences for the controversy of Zion” (Isaiah 34:8). Edom had rejoiced at Jerusalem's fall. God answered for His people. The land soaked with blood is the terrible picture of what it means for God to plead the cause of Zion.

corruption_summary: Prophecies like Isaiah 34 are dismissed as primitive tribal vengeance, when they reveal the holy justice of God that the cross alone answers for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: The prophecy of Edom's judgment offends a sentimental view of God, and many modern readers set the God of the prophets against the God of Jesus. That is the old Marcionite error. Christ Himself spoke of the coming wrath, and Revelation 19 borrows Isaiah's imagery of the treading of the winepress.

The principle to recover is the reality of divine vengeance and the refuge from it. The day of the LORD'S vengeance falls on every enemy of Zion, and the only shelter is the blood of the Lamb, shed for His people.

pos: v.t. (to press and move along a surface with the hands)
etymology: Middle English rubben, of Low German origin. In Luke 6:1 the participle rubbing renders the Greek psocho, to rub in the hands.
biblical_def: On a sabbath the Lord walked through the grain fields with His disciples. “And it came to pass on the second sabbath after the first, that he went through the corn fields; and his disciples plucked the ears of corn, and did eat, rubbing them in their hands” (Luke 6:1). The law expressly allowed it: “When thou comest into the standing corn of thy neighbour, then thou mayest pluck the ears with thine hand; but thou shalt not move a sickle unto thy neighbour's standing corn” (Deuteronomy 23:25). But the Pharisees counted plucking as reaping and rubbing as threshing: “And certain of the Pharisees said unto them, Why do ye that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days?” (Luke 6:2). Christ answered from David and the shewbread, and declared Himself Lord also of the sabbath. Rubbing grain in the hand was not work against God's law; it was hunger satisfied under it, and the charge was the Pharisees' own tradition.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RUB, verb transitive [Latin probrum, exprobro; Gr. to rub We have the elements of the word in scrape, scrub, Latin scribo, Gr.] 1. To move something along the surface of a body with pressure; as, to rub the face or arms with the hand;
webster_full: RUB, verb transitive [Latin probrum, exprobro; Gr. to rub We have the elements of the word in scrape, scrub, Latin scribo, Gr.] 1. To move something along the surface of a body with pressure; as, to rub the face or arms with the hand; to rub the body with flannel. Vessels are scoured or cleaned by rubbing them.
2. To wipe; to clean; to scour; but rub is a generic term, applicable to friction for every purpose.
3. To touch so as to leave behind something which touches; to spread over; as to rub any thing with oil.
4. To polish; to retouch; with over. The whole business of our redemption is to rub over the defaced copy of the creation.

5. To obstruct by collision. [Unusual.] In popular language, rub is used for teasing, fretting, upbraiding, reproaching or vexing with gibes or sarcasms. To rub down, to clean by rubbing; to comb or curry, as a horse. To rub off, to clean any thing by rubbing; to separate by friction; as, to rub off rust.
scriptures: Luk 6:1
And it came to pass on the second sabbath after the first, that he went through the corn fields; and his disciples plucked the ears of corn, and did eat, rubbing them in their hands.
Luk 6:2
And certain of the Pharisees said unto them, Why do ye that which is not lawful to do on the sabbath days?
When thou comest into the standing corn of thy neighbour, then thou mayest pluck the ears with thine hand; but thou shalt not move a sickle unto thy neighbour's standing corn.
corruption_summary: The episode is used to argue that Christ abolished the sabbath, when He defended its true use against human additions and claimed lordship over it.
corruption_paragraphs: Many read the grain-field controversy as Jesus setting aside the fourth commandment. He did the opposite: He appealed to Scripture against tradition, and He declared that the sabbath was made for man. The 1689 Confession, chapter 22, holds that the Christian sabbath, the Lord's day, remains a perpetual moral command, kept holy to the Lord, with works of necessity and mercy permitted.

The principle to recover is the distinction between God's law and men's traditions. The disciples' rubbing was a work of necessity, allowed by the law; the Pharisees bound the conscience where God had left it free.

pos: v.t. (to peck, pluck out, as a bird with its beak)
etymology: Middle English picken, perhaps from Old Norse pikka, to peck. In Proverbs 30:17 it renders the Hebrew naqar, to bore, pick out, gouge.
biblical_def: Agur's collection includes one of the most vivid warnings in Proverbs. “The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it” (Proverbs 30:17). The eye is singled out because contempt begins with a look, the rolled eye and the scornful glance. The punishment fits it: the eye that despised is left unburied in the valley for the birds. The proverb rests on the fifth commandment: “Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee” (Exodus 20:12). Long life is promised to the honouring child; a shameful death is threatened to the mocking one. Solomon gives the positive counsel: “Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old” (Proverbs 23:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): PICK, verb transitive [Latin pecto.] 1. To pull off or pluck with the fingers something that grows or adheres to another thing; to separate by the hand, as fruit from trees; as, to pick apples or oranges; to pick strawberries.

2. To pull off or separate with the teeth, beak or claws; as, to pick flesh from a bone; hence,
3. To clean by the teeth, fingers or claws, or by a small instrument, by separating something that adheres; as, to pick a bone; to pick the ears.
4. To take up; to cause or seek industriously; as, to pick a quarrel.
5. To separate or pull asunder; to pull into small parcels by the fingers; to separate locks for loosening and cleaning; as, to pick wool.

corruption_summary: Honouring parents is reduced to a conditional courtesy owed only to parents who earn it, when the commandment binds children to honour the office God gave their father and mother.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary counsel often teaches that respect must be earned and that children owe their parents honour only so far as they find them worthy. The fifth commandment is not written that way. It addresses the child, names the father and the mother, and attaches a promise; the Larger Catechism expounds it as reverence, obedience and gratitude toward all superiors in their place.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the order of the household under God. The mocking eye is a sin against the God who set the child under the parent.

pos: v.i. (to flow in drops or a thin stream)
etymology: Middle English triklen, perhaps a variant of strikelen, frequentative of striken, to flow. In Lamentations 3:49 it renders the Hebrew nagar, to flow, pour out, run down.
biblical_def: Jeremiah's grief over Jerusalem is the grief of a man who never stops weeping. “Mine eye runneth down with rivers of water for the destruction of the daughter of my people” (Lamentations 3:48). The rivers become a steady trickle that will not cease: “Mine eye trickleth down, and ceaseth not, without any intermission” (Lamentations 3:49). But the tears have a limit, and it is not exhaustion; it is God: “Till the LORD look down, and behold from heaven” (Lamentations 3:50). The prophet weeps in hope. He has already written the great confession at the centre of the book, that the LORD'S mercies are new every morning. His tears trickle on because he waits for God to look, and he believes God will.

pos: n. pl. (ceremonial ablutions of the law)
etymology: From wash, Old English wascan, plus -ing. In Hebrews 9:10 it renders the Greek baptismoi, washings, immersions, ritual cleansings.
biblical_def: Hebrews explains why the old covenant's rites could not cleanse the conscience. The tabernacle and its services were a figure for the time then present, “Which stood only in meats and drinks, and divers washings, and carnal ordinances, imposed on them until the time of reformation” (Hebrews 9:10). The law commanded many washings: of priests, of vessels, of the unclean. Tradition added more, as Mark observes of the Pharisees: “And many other things there be, which they have received to hold, as the washing of cups, and pots, brasen vessels, and of tables” (Mark 7:4). All of them touched the body; none reached the heart. Christ's blood does what they pictured, and the believer now draws near on that ground: “Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22). The divers washings were imposed until the time of reformation, and the reformation has come in Christ.

Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
corruption_summary: Rome restored a system of ritual washings, holy water, lavabo and sprinkling, as means of grace, when Hebrews says such washings were imposed only until Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman church uses holy water at church doors, in blessings and in the rite of sprinkling, and teaches that such sacramentals dispose the soul to grace and remit venial sin. Hebrews 9:10 classes washings with meats and drinks as carnal ordinances belonging to the time before the reformation that Christ accomplished.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Christ's blood and the simplicity of New Testament worship. The church has one washing appointed by Christ, baptism, which signifies cleansing but does not effect it by the outward act, and no other ritual ablution is commanded.

pos: proper n. (rugged region south of Damascus, part of Philip’s tetrarchy)
etymology: Greek Trachonitis, from trachon, a rough, stony tract, from trachus, rough: the rugged country; the lava plateau now called the Leja.
biblical_def: Trachonitis is named once, beside Ituraea, in Luke's synchronism: “and his brother Philip tetrarch of Ituraea and of the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene” (Luke 3:1). The district was a broken lava field south of Damascus, a natural fortress long infested by robbers, which Augustus gave to Herod the Great to pacify and which passed to Philip. Philip's capital lay in the same tetrarchy, and it was there that the Lord asked His disciples the question on which everything turns: “When Jesus came into the coasts of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?” (Matthew 16:13). Peter's answer was given in Philip's territory: “Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16). Luke names the rough country to fix a date; Matthew shows that the greatest confession of the Gospels was made under the same tetrarch's rule.

etymology: From in and side, Old English side, a flank. In 1 Kings 6:15 it renders the Hebrew bayith, house, used for the interior, within.
biblical_def: Solomon's temple was stone without and cedar and gold within. “And he built the walls of the house within with boards of cedar, both the floor of the house, and the walls of the cieling: and he covered them on the inside with wood, and covered the floor of the house with planks of fir” (1 Kings 6:15). No stone could be seen from the inside: “And the cedar of the house within was carved with knops and open flowers: all was cedar; there was no stone seen” (1 Kings 6:18). Then the cedar itself was overlaid: “And the floor of the house he overlaid with gold, within and without” (1 Kings 6:30). The glory of the house was hidden inside, where only the priests went. The pattern runs through Scripture: God looks on the heart, and Christ rebuked those who cleansed the outside of the cup while the inside was full of extortion. The true temple is beautiful within.

etymology: From there and about. In Luke 24:4 it renders the Greek peri toutou, concerning this.
biblical_def: The women came to the tomb with spices and found the stone rolled away. “And they entered in, and found not the body of the Lord Jesus” (Luke 24:3). Their confusion is recorded in one old word: “And it came to pass, as they were much perplexed thereabout, behold, two men stood by them in shining garments” (Luke 24:4). Webster cites the verse for the sense concerning that. The perplexity was answered by a question and a reminder: “Why seek ye the living among the dead?” (Luke 24:5). “He is not here, but is risen: remember how he spake unto you when he was yet in Galilee” (Luke 24:6). The women had been perplexed thereabout because they had forgotten His words. The resurrection did not surprise the Lord's prophecy; it surprised the Lord's friends, and the cure for their perplexity was to remember what He had said.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): THEREABOUT, THEREABOUTS, adverb [there and about.] 1. Near that place. 2. Nearly; near that number, degree or quantity. 3. Concerning that. Luke 24:4.
webster_full: THEREABOUT ', THEREABOUTS ', adverb [there and about. The latter is less proper, but most commonly used.]
1. Near that place.
2. Nearly; near that number, degree or quantity; as ten men or thereabouts.
3. Concerning that. [Not much used.] Luke 24:4.
In Luke 24:4 it renders the Greek peri toutou, concerning this.

corruption_paragraphs: The word is plain. The empty tomb narratives are dismissed by skeptics as legend, but the honest record of the women's perplexity, and of the apostles' disbelief of their report, is not how legends are written.
This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bodily resurrection of Christ, and the remedy for doubt: remember how He spake.
